query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermal treatment that promotes the in-situ formation of coherent nanoprecipitates along the lamellar internal boundaries will improve room‐temperature tensile ductility and reduce brittleness in the eutectic HEA while retaining or increasing its strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical dual-phase (lamellar) microstructure composed of alternating soft (fcc) and hard (ordered/bcc) colonies that suffer from dislocation pile-ups at internal phase boundaries.
generation.intervention: Perform a carefully optimized isothermal annealing treatment (or short heat-treatment cycle) designed to induce fine, coherent nanoprecipitation along the internal lamellar boundaries.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing under quasi-static loading; microstructural examination using TEM/SEM after annealing; the heat treatment conditions (temperature and time) should be selected to ensure coherent precipitates without coarsening the lamellae.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent nanoprecipitates decorating the lamellar boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The nanoprecipitates form coherent interfaces at the internal boundaries, which facilitate dislocation transmission across phases and reduce dislocation pile-ups. This alleviation of local stress concentrations minimizes premature microcracking and catastrophic damage during straining while providing precipitation strengthening to maintain or enhance the overall strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated material is expected to exhibit a significant increase in ductility (through more homogeneous plastic deformation and decreased tendency for microcracking) while retaining or slightly increasing yield and ultimate tensile strengths compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated eutectic HEA exhibiting limited room-temperature ductility and brittleness due to dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: The improvement will be effective only if the induced nanoprecipitates remain coherent and finely distributed; excessive coarsening or incoherency would not alleviate stress concentrations and could even be detrimental.
generation.uncertainty: The precise heat treatment parameters (temperature, time, cooling rate) required to optimize the nanoprecipitate size and distribution are not yet determined, and quantitative changes in strength and ductility (percentage improvements) remain to be experimentally validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the eutectic HEA. One set receives the optimized isothermal annealing treatment to induce coherent nanoprecipitates; the other remains as-cast or receives a standard heat treatment without nanoprecipitate formation. Conduct identical room-temperature tensile tests while assessing microstructure (via TEM/SEM) to observe nanoprecipitate formation and dislocation behavior.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
TEM/SEM analysis of lamellar boundaries for nanoprecipitate size, density, and coherency
Fractography to assess the nature and initiation of cracks
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a significant increase in tensile ductility (or show similar or reduced ductility) and the microstructural study does not reveal the presence of coherent nanoprecipitates at internal boundaries compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.
